claim: A multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) global table must be deployed in exactly three Regions: either three replicas, or two replicas and one witness.
question: How many Regions does an MRSC global table use, and can one of them be a witness?

qualifiers.condition: a witness holds data but cannot be read or written

evidence.quote: A MRSC global table must be deployed in exactly three Regions. You can configure a MRSC global table with three replicas, or with two replicas and one witness.

claim: In an MRSC global table, item changes are synchronously replicated to at least one other Region before the write returns success, and a strongly consistent read on any MRSC replica returns the latest version of an item.
question: How does MRSC replicate writes, and what do strongly consistent reads return?

values.display: synchronously replicated to at least one other Region
values.spoken: synchronously replicated to at least one other Region

values.display: always return the latest version of an item

evidence.quote: Item changes in an MRSC global table replica are synchronously replicated to at least one other Region before the write operation returns a successful response. Strongly consistent read operations on any MRSC replica always return the latest version of an item.

claim: MRSC global tables support a recovery point objective (RPO) of zero but have higher write and strongly consistent read latencies than MREC. MREC global tables have an RPO equal to the replication delay between replicas, usually a few seconds.
question: Which global tables mode gives an RPO of zero, and what RPO does the eventual-consistency mode give?

qualifiers.condition: the consistency mode is chosen at creation and cannot be changed

evidence.quote: MRSC global tables will have higher write and strongly consistent read latencies compared to MREC global tables. MRSC global tables support a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of zero.
MREC global tables have a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) equal to the replication delay between replicas, usually a few seconds depending on the replica Regions.

claim: Multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC) is the default mode for a new global table. Writes are replicated asynchronously, typically within a second or less, and conflicts on the same item are resolved by last writer wins.
question: What is the default global table consistency mode, and how are concurrent writes in different Regions resolved?

values.display: typically within a second or less
values.spoken: typically within a second or less

qualifiers.condition: a global table cannot mix modes and the mode cannot be changed after creation

evidence.quote: Multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC) is the default consistency mode for global tables. Item changes in an MREC global table replica are asynchronously replicated to all other replicas, typically within a second or less.

If the same item is modified in multiple Regions simultaneously, DynamoDB will resolve the conflict by using the modification with the latest internal timestamp on a per-item basis, referred to as a "last writer wins" conflict resolution method.

claim: MRSC global tables do not support Time to Live (TTL), local secondary indexes (LSIs) or transaction operations; a transaction on an MRSC replica returns an error.
question: Which DynamoDB features are not supported on MRSC global tables?

values.display: Time to Live (TTL) is not supported
Local secondary indexes (LSIs) are not supported

evidence.quote: Time to Live (TTL) is not supported for MRSC global tables.
Local secondary indexes (LSIs) are not supported for MRSC global tables.
Global tables configured for multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) do not support transaction operations, and will return an error if those operations are invoked on an MRSC replica.

claim: On June 30, 2025 multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) for global tables became generally available, with an optional witness Region and a recovery point objective of zero. Before MRSC, global tables were eventually consistent; MRSC was announced in preview on December 3, 2024.
question: When did DynamoDB global tables get multi-Region strong consistency, and what does it add?

qualifiers.condition: exactly three Regions; three replicas or two replicas and one witness

evidence.quote: | [Added Multi-Region Strong Consistency (MRSC) support for DynamoDB global tables](#DocumentHistory) | DynamoDB now supports Multi-Region Strong Consistency (MRSC) for global tables with optional witness Region. MRSC allows strongly consistent reads across Regions with a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of zero during regional failures. MRSC global tables must be deployed in exactly three Regions, with either three replicas or two replicas and one witness. For more information and available Regions, see [Multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/V2globaltables_HowItWorks.html#V2globaltables_HowItWorks.consistency-modes.html). | June 30, 2025 |

| [DynamoDB global tables now supports multi-Region strong consistency](#DocumentHistory) | With multi-Region strong consistency, you can build highly available multi-Region applications with a recovery point objective (RPO) of zero, achieving the highest level of resilience. For more information, see [Global tables with multi-Region strong consistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/multi-region-strong-consistency-gt.html). | December 3, 2024 |

claim: In September 2026 MRSC global tables expanded to five additional Regions (Canada (Central), Europe (Stockholm), Europe (Spain), Asia Pacific (Mumbai) and Asia Pacific (Singapore)), for 15 supported Regions in total, with any three-Region configuration allowed, including across continents.
question: What changed for MRSC global tables Regions in September 2026?

values.display: total number of supported Regions to 15
any three-Region configuration across the 15 supported AWS Regions
values.spoken: any three of the fifteen Regions

qualifiers.condition: announced after the exam cutoff of the book

evidence.quote: Starting today, Amazon DynamoDB global tables with multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) is available in five additional AWS Regions: Canada (Central), Europe (Stockholm), Europe (Spain), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), and Asia Pacific (Singapore), bringing the total number of supported Regions to 15.
You can now create an MRSC global table in any three-Region configuration across the 15 supported AWS Regions, configured with either three replicas or two replicas and one witness Region.

claim: Multi-account global tables are supported for multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC) global tables only; MRSC global tables do not support the multi-account model. Each replica must be in a separate AWS account.
question: Which global table consistency mode supports replicas in different AWS accounts?

values.display: supported for multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC) global tables
Each replica must reside in a separate AWS account

qualifiers.condition: a table with N replicas needs N accounts

evidence.quote: Multi-account replication is supported for multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC) global tables.
Each replica must reside in a separate AWS account.
Global tables configured for [Multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC)](V2globaltables_HowItWorks.md#V2globaltables_HowItWorks.consistency-modes.mrsc) do not support the multi-account model.

claim: For multi-account global tables, customers must provide replication permissions to the DynamoDB global tables service principal in their resource policies, and table settings such as throughput mode and TTL are shared by all replicas and cannot be overridden per replica.
question: What must you grant for multi-account global tables, and can settings differ per replica?

values.display: replication permissions to the DynamoDB global tables service principal in their resource policies
values.spoken: grant the global tables service principal in resource policies

evidence.quote: Customers must provide replication permissions to the DynamoDB global tables service principal in their resource policies.
Multi-account global tables use unified table settings across all replicas by default.
All replicas automatically share the same configuration (such as throughput mode and TTL), and unlike same-account global tables, these settings cannot be overridden per replica.

claim: On February 3, 2026 DynamoDB global tables gained replication across multiple AWS accounts, so replicas can be in different accounts and Regions for account-level isolation, instead of replicas in one account only.
question: When did global tables start to support replicas in different AWS accounts?

evidence.quote: Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support replication across multiple AWS accounts.
With this new capability, you can replicate tables across AWS accounts and Regions to improve resiliency, isolate workloads at the account level, and apply distinct security and governance controls.
